title: Feminist Epistemology and Philosophy of Science

summaries.example: Imagine a class choosing a playground problem to study. If only the students who use the soccer field are asked, the class may miss problems near the swings. If students with different experiences can speak and everyone listens carefully, the class may learn more. Feminist epistemology asks similar questions about who gets to join inquiry, whose knowledge is trusted, and which questions are asked.
summaries.summary: Feminist epistemology studies how gender and other social relationships can affect knowledge. It asks who is allowed to investigate, who is believed, what questions are considered important, and whether common ideas about objectivity leave out some people. The entry explains three main approaches. Standpoint theory considers whether people who face subordination can have useful or sometimes advantaged perspectives on the systems affecting them. Feminist postmodernism warns against treating “women” as one identical group and stresses that people have many, changing identities and viewpoints. Feminist empiricism keeps a strong role for evidence but argues that values and social perspectives can help investigators find important questions and explanations. These approaches increasingly overlap. Together, they support inquiry that is open to criticism, includes people from different positions, and recognizes that knowledge may be partial without being useless or merely a matter of opinion. The entry also examines unfair credibility judgments, socially produced ignorance, and ways to make science and other inquiry more responsive and fair.
key_ideas: People can notice different things because their experiences and social positions differ.
Some knowledge practices have excluded women and other groups, ignored their questions, or treated them as less trustworthy.
Standpoint theory explores whether people in less powerful positions may notice parts of social life that powerful groups overlook.
Postmodern approaches emphasize that there is no single, simple viewpoint that speaks for every woman.
Feminist empiricism argues that evidence matters while also asking how values, background assumptions, and research communities shape inquiry.
Better inquiry can include more voices, welcome criticism, and examine whose interests knowledge serves.
summaries.why_it_matters: What we learn can affect people’s lives. If researchers leave out certain groups or assume that one group’s experience is everyone’s experience, important problems may remain hidden. Feminist epistemology encourages careful questions about evidence, participation, fairness, and the uses of knowledge. It does not simply reject science or objectivity; many feminist philosophers seek better inquiry through wider participation, public criticism, and attention to overlooked evidence.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge: how people know things, what counts as good reasons, and who is treated as a knower.
The idea that what someone knows can be shaped by their body, experiences, social position, and relationships with others.
A person or group being accepted as someone whose information and judgment deserve attention.
Unfair treatment that harms someone as a knower, such as ignoring their testimony because of prejudice.
A way of investigating a question and checking whether an answer is well supported.

questions_to_think_about: Who gets listened to when a group solves a problem?
Can having an experience help someone notice something others miss?
How can a group check whether an unfair stereotype is affecting its judgment?
Should people with different experiences work together when investigating a question?

summaries.example: Suppose researchers study why some students leave an advanced science program. One study might focus on students’ personal choices. A feminist approach could also ask how scheduling, caregiving expectations, financial pressures, classroom norms, and judgments about who “looks like” a scientist shape participation. These are not automatically competing explanations. Researchers must compare them with evidence, while recognizing that their interests helped determine which causes they investigated and which outcomes they considered important.
summaries.summary: Feminist epistemology and philosophy of science examine how gender and other social relations shape knowledge, inquiry, and judgments of credibility. The central idea of situated knowledge is that knowers encounter the world from embodied and social positions that affect access to information, interpretation, interests, background assumptions, and relations with other inquirers. The entry develops three major approaches. Feminist standpoint theory argues that subordinated positions can sometimes reveal social structures, their changeability, and the interests they serve, but later versions reject the idea that all women share one standpoint or possess automatic authority. Feminist postmodernism challenges essentialism and universal “woman” categories, emphasizing multiple, shifting perspectives and the need to acknowledge responsibility for how representations are made. Feminist empiricism retains the importance of experience and evidence while arguing that inquiry is theory-laden, social, and influenced by values. Values can shape questions, classifications, methods, models, and standards of proof without replacing empirical testing. These approaches increasingly converge around local, plural, fallible inquiry. Feminist criticisms of objectivity target ideals such as a view from nowhere, emotional detachment, value-neutrality, and control when these ideals conceal situated choices or privilege dominant interests. Alternative accounts emphasize reflexivity, inclusion, democratic criticism, and equality of intellectual authority. The entry also analyzes testimonial and hermeneutical injustice, socially organized ignorance, and epistemic virtues such as open-mindedness and fair credibility assessment. External critics worry that feminist inquiry confuses facts and values;
key_ideas: Social location can affect access to information, interpretation, standards of justification, and who is treated as authoritative; this does not mean every belief from a particular group is automatically true.
Standpoint theorists have moved away from a single standpoint of all women toward plural, intersecting standpoints and more limited, problem-specific advantages.

Feminist postmodernists criticize essentialism: the assumption that women share one fixed nature or one unified viewpoint. They also emphasize perspective-shifting and responsibility for one’s representations.

Feminist empiricists reject the idea that all values necessarily corrupt inquiry. Values may guide questions, classifications, methods, standards of proof, models, and explanations, while evidence remains essential for testing claims.

Because theories are often underdetermined by evidence, inquiry can be pluralistic. Different research programs may reveal different patterns, provided they remain open to criticism and avoid clear error or dogmatism.

Feminist accounts of objectivity often focus on procedures: public criticism, democratic participation, reflexivity about situatedness, and equal intellectual standing can help expose partial or biased conclusions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because research and public knowledge influence institutions, technologies, health decisions, education, and social policy. Examining who participates and whose experiences count can reveal questions and harms that dominant research has missed. The feminist approaches described in the entry do not have one single program, and they do not simply discard science or truth. Their shared challenge is to make inquiry more self-aware, inclusive, evidence-responsive, and capable of correcting the effects of social power.

important_terms.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with knowledge, justification, knowers, and the practices through which beliefs are investigated and defended.
Knowledge understood as reflecting a knower’s embodied, social, historical, and relational position rather than coming from a completely positionless viewpoint.
A socially located perspective claimed to offer some epistemic advantage for particular questions, often concerning relations of power and subordination.
An approach skeptical of universal or fixed accounts of gender and knowledge; it emphasizes plurality, contingency, shifting identities, and the role of language and social practices.
An approach that gives experience and empirical investigation a central role while examining how social values, background assumptions, and scientific communities shape inquiry.
The claim that evidence alone may not determine one theory, because background assumptions and interpretive choices help connect observations with hypotheses.
Unfairly treating someone’s contribution as less credible or less intelligible because of prejudice or exclusion from meaning-making practices.
A model of objectivity in which inquiry becomes more reliable through public criticism, reflexivity, inclusion, and equality of intellectual authority.

questions_to_think_about: When does a socially marginalized position provide useful access to information, and when would claiming automatic privilege be unjustified?
Can values help investigators ask better questions without allowing them to ignore inconvenient evidence?
What is gained, and what might be lost, by treating gender as intersecting with race, class, sexuality, and other identities?
How could a research community distinguish legitimate differences in expertise from illegitimate exercises of social power?
Is a theory more objective because it is detached, or because it survives criticism from diverse and accountable investigators?

summaries.example: A school wants to learn why some students do not join the robotics club. If it asks only current club members, it may hear that the club is welcoming. Students who stayed away might describe meeting times, costs, teasing, or the feeling that robotics is “for” a certain kind of student. Neither set of voices should automatically settle the question. A careful investigation would include both groups, examine evidence, and ask how the club’s structure affects different students.
summaries.summary: Feminist epistemology asks how gender and social power influence knowing. It studies who is included in inquiry, who is believed, which questions are treated as important, and how scientific methods and ideas of objectivity can be improved. Its central concept, situated knowledge, means that knowers approach the world from particular bodies, histories, roles, relationships, and interests. Standpoint theory explores whether people who are subordinated can have an especially useful perspective on the systems that disadvantage them. However, feminist thinkers have criticized the idea of one unified standpoint of women, since gender intersects with race, class, sexuality, and other identities. Feminist postmodernism stresses that identities and meanings are shaped by social practices and that no viewpoint can claim to rise completely above all perspectives. Feminist empiricism gives evidence a central place but argues that evidence does not interpret itself: background assumptions and values help determine which questions are asked, how phenomena are classified, and which explanations are developed. The entry therefore considers whether values can be epistemic resources rather than merely sources of error. It also examines criticisms of traditional objectivity, including the ideals of total detachment, neutrality, and a “view from nowhere.” Feminist alternatives emphasize reflexivity, plural methods, inclusion, public criticism, and fair relations among knowers. Finally, the entry discusses epistemic injustice, in which prejudice harms people’s credibility or ability to make sense of their experiences, as well as socially produced ignorance and virtues that can help repair these problems.
key_ideas: People’s social locations can influence what information they can access and how others respond to what they say.
Standpoint theory asks whether groups with less power can notice hidden rules or harms that dominant groups overlook, but it does not require believing every member of a group thinks alike.
Feminist postmodernism criticizes one-size-fits-all theories of women and emphasizes intersecting identities and many changing perspectives.
Feminist empiricism argues that values can guide useful questions and methods without replacing evidence or protecting a theory from criticism.
The three approaches began as different traditions but have increasingly shared ideas about plural perspectives, fallibility, and local investigation.
Objectivity may improve when researchers explain their own positions, include marginalized participants, and create real opportunities for criticism.
summaries.why_it_matters: Knowledge is not made in a vacuum. Decisions based on research can shape whose needs are noticed and whose problems remain invisible. Feminist epistemology gives students tools for examining sources, institutions, and scientific practices without treating every claim as equally good or dismissing evidence. It asks how inquiry can become more reliable by making hidden assumptions visible, inviting criticism from different social positions, and preventing power from deciding in advance who counts as an expert.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of knowledge, including how beliefs are supported and who is recognized as a reliable knower.
Knowledge shaped by the knower’s experiences, body, social position, relationships, and interests.
A perspective that may give a group a useful advantage for understanding particular social conditions, especially conditions of disadvantage.
The belief that a category, such as “women,” has one universal and unchanging nature or viewpoint.
The view that evidence is central to knowledge, while inquiry is also affected by theories, values, and social practices.
The unfair downgrading of someone’s credibility or ability to contribute because of prejudice or exclusion.
The idea that different background assumptions can make the same observations support different explanations.
A process for checking ideas through open criticism, participation, and fair treatment of contributors.

questions_to_think_about: Why might people in different roles notice different problems in the same organization?
What is the difference between saying a perspective may be useful and saying it is always correct?
How can a research project include values while still testing its claims against evidence?
What happens when a group lacks the words or concepts needed to describe an experience?
Should every viewpoint receive equal authority, or should expertise also matter?
